note: Questions from the CBSE Class XII Biology board exam 2023, Q.P. code 57/1/1, published by CBSE at cbse.gov.in. Q6 (DNA fingerprint image) is left out and other figures are described in words; case study Q29 is regrouped into parts that each total 4 marks. Solutions are written for this portal and are not CBSE's official marking scheme.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following processes results in the production of recombinants in future generations? (i) Mutation (ii) Independent assortment during meiosis I (iii) Independent assortment during meiosis II (iv) Crossing over of bivalents
questions.solution: New combinations arise from independent assortment of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I and from crossing over between them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A schematic diagram of prokaryotic transcription shows a region X on the DNA where a factor Y, attached to an enzyme Z, binds to start transcription. Identify X, Y and Z.
questions.solution: RNA polymerase binds the promoter with the help of the sigma initiation factor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A human age pyramid is widest in the reproductive age group, with fewer individuals in the pre-reproductive group than in the reproductive group, and fewest in the post-reproductive group. The status of the population is :
questions.solution: An urn-shaped pyramid with a narrow pre-reproductive base indicates a declining population.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Students measured dissolved oxygen and mineral ions along a river flowing outside their city. At points (i) to (iii) dissolved oxygen rises and mineral ions fall, but at point (iv) dissolved oxygen starts to fall sharply while mineral ions rise. Which point indicates the entry of untreated sewage into the river?
questions.solution: Sewage brings organic matter and nutrients; microbes decomposing it use up dissolved oxygen (high BOD), so DO falls and minerals rise.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Match the enzymes with their functions: P. DNA ligase Q. Restriction exonuclease R. Taq polymerase S. Restriction endonuclease — i. Removes nucleotides from ends of DNA ii. Extends primer on a DNA template iii. Joins the DNA fragments iv. Cuts DNA at a specific position
questions.solution: Ligase joins fragments, exonucleases remove end nucleotides, Taq polymerase extends primers in PCR and endonucleases cut at specific positions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A graph of the number of giraffes against neck length is a bell-shaped curve with its peak at medium neck length. Select the option that correctly describes the process of natural selection shown.
options: Stabilising selection as giraffes with longer neck lengths are selected further.
Disruptive selection as giraffes with smaller and longer neck lengths are selected.
Directional selection as giraffes with longer neck lengths are selected.
Stabilising selection as giraffes with medium neck lengths are selected.
questions.solution: In stabilising selection, individuals with the mean value of the character are favoured.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Choose the correct number of pollen grains that will be formed after 325 microspore mother cells undergo microsporogenesis.
questions.solution: Each microspore mother cell gives a tetrad of 4 pollen grains: 325 × 4 = 1300.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Match the contraceptive devices with their modes of action: P. Lippes loop Q. Multiload 375 R. Subcutaneous Norplant S. Saheli — i. Inhibition of ovulation ii. Phagocytosis of sperms in uterus iii. Causes thickening of cervical mucus iv. Makes cervix hostile to sperms
questions.solution: Non-medicated IUDs (Lippes loop) increase phagocytosis of sperms; copper IUDs (Multiload) make the cervix hostile to sperms; implants thicken cervical mucus; Saheli acts mainly by inhibiting ovulation (as matched in the paper).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In which option does the endocrine gland correctly match its hormone and function?
options: Sertoli cells – testosterone – development of secondary sexual characteristics
Placenta – estrogen – initiates secretion of milk
Leydig cells – androgen – initiates the production of sperms
questions.solution: Leydig cells secrete androgens, which stimulate spermatogenesis. Testosterone is from Leydig cells, and FSH from the pituitary.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The organism used in the construction of the first artificial recombinant DNA by Cohen and Boyer in 1972 was :
questions.solution: They linked an antibiotic resistance gene to a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Who challenged the patent right granted to the University of Mississippi Medical Centre for 'use of turmeric in wound healing'?
questions.solution: The challenge was led by CSIR under Dr. R.A. Mashelkar, and the patent was revoked.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): A patient of ADA deficiency undergoing gene therapy requires periodic infusion of genetically engineered lymphocytes.
Reason (R): Lymphocytes are immortal.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Lymphocytes are not immortal, which is why periodic infusion is needed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): A cattle egret and grazing cattle in close association is a classic example of commensalism.
Reason (R): As grazing cattle move through the field, they stir up and flush out insects from the vegetation that otherwise might be difficult for egrets to find and catch.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: The egret benefits while the cattle are neither benefited nor harmed.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Endosperm is completely consumed during the development of the embryo in ex-albuminous seeds.
Reason (R): Castor, pea and beans are all examples of ex-albuminous seeds.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Castor is albuminous (it retains endosperm), so R is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Birds like pigeons have heterogametic females whereas the males are homogametic.
Reason (R): In pigeons, females have Z and W sex chromosomes whereas males have ZZ sex chromosomes.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Females producing Z and W eggs are heterogametic, which is exactly what R states.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A diagram shows a developmental stage of the human embryo: a hollow ball with an outer layer of cells X and a group of cells Y attached to the inside at one end. (a) Identify the stage. (b) Mention its exact location in a normal pregnancy. (c) Write one function each of X and Y.
questions.solution: (a) Blastocyst. (b) It gets implanted in the endometrium (wall) of the uterus. (c) X is the trophoblast, which attaches to the endometrium and helps form the placenta. Y is the inner cell mass, which differentiates into the embryo.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) From which end of the ovule, and how, does the pollen tube gain entry into the embryo sac of a Hibiscus flower? (b) State the fate of the male nuclei present in the pollen tube.
questions.solution: (a) Through the micropyle; it enters one of the synergids, guided by the filiform apparatus. (b) One male gamete fuses with the egg (syngamy) to form the diploid zygote; the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion) to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus. Together this is double fertilisation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Identify structure A (a circular double-stranded DNA molecule) and structure B (a virus with a polyhedral head containing DNA, a tail and tail fibres). (ii) State their importance in biotechnology experiments.
questions.solution: (i) A: plasmid; B: bacteriophage. (ii) Both are used as cloning vectors: they replicate in bacterial cells and can carry and multiply a foreign DNA fragment linked to them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Explain the process by which a bacterial cell can be made 'competent' to take up foreign DNA from its surroundings, using divalent cations and temperature treatment.
questions.solution: Bacterial cells are treated with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium, which increases the efficiency with which DNA enters through pores in the cell wall. The cells are incubated with the recombinant DNA on ice, given a brief heat shock at 42 °C, and put back on ice; this makes them take up the DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Ecological pyramids give important information about the ecological system, but have some limitations. List any two limitations of ecological pyramids.
questions.solution: They do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain, which rarely exists, and do not accommodate food webs; saprophytes are not given any place although they play a vital role.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: India is the seventh largest country in the world. Write the value of the land area of our country (in terms of percentage) of the world. Mention what makes India one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world.
questions.solution: India has only 2.4% of the world's land area, but its share of global species diversity is about 8.1%, which makes it one of the 12 mega-diversity countries.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: With the help of a schematic diagram only, show in three steps the formation of recombinant DNA by the action of the restriction endonuclease EcoRI and DNA ligase.
questions.solution: Step 1: EcoRI cuts the vector DNA and the foreign DNA at the same site, 5′-G↓AATTC-3′, on both strands. Step 2: both get complementary sticky ends (single-stranded AATT overhangs). Step 3: the sticky ends of the foreign DNA and vector pair up, and DNA ligase seals the gaps, giving recombinant DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A pedigree: unaffected parents (Gen I) have three children — an unaffected son 1, who marries an affected woman; an affected son 2; and an unaffected daughter 3, who marries an unaffected man. Son 1 and his affected wife have an unaffected daughter. Daughter 3 and her husband have an affected son and two unaffected daughters (Gen III). (a) Is the trait dominant or recessive? Give reason. (b) Is it autosomal or sex-linked? Give reason. (c) Write the possible genotypes of children 1 and 3 of the second generation.
questions.solution: (a) Recessive: unaffected parents have an affected son, and unaffected daughter 3 has an affected son, so the trait is carried by unaffected individuals. (b) Sex-linked (X-linked recessive): affected individuals born in the family are males, and the trait passes from an unaffected (carrier) mother to her son. (c) Child 1 (son): XY (normal). Child 3 (daughter): XᵃX, a carrier.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Write the characteristics of stem cells. (b) From where can stem cells be obtained in humans? (c) State any two applications of stem cells in curing human diseases.
questions.solution: (a) They are undifferentiated cells that can divide repeatedly (self-renew) and can differentiate into specialised cell types. (b) From embryos (inner cell mass), umbilical cord blood and bone marrow. (c) Treating blood cancers such as leukaemia and other blood disorders by bone marrow transplant; repairing or regenerating damaged tissues and organs, for example in diabetes, spinal injuries or heart damage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Differentiate between malignant and benign tumours. (b) Name and explain the most feared property of a malignant tumour.
questions.solution: (a) Benign tumours stay confined to their original location, do not spread and cause little damage. Malignant tumours are masses of proliferating neoplastic cells that grow rapidly, invade and damage surrounding tissues. (b) Metastasis: cells sloughed from the tumour travel through the blood to distant sites and start new tumours wherever they lodge.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Explain the following with reference to wastewater treatment : (a) primary sludge (b) activated sludge (c) anaerobic sludge digesters
questions.solution: (a) In primary treatment, floating debris is removed by filtration and grit by sedimentation; the solids that settle form the primary sludge. (b) In secondary treatment, the effluent is aerated so that aerobic microbes grow as flocs and consume organic matter; when BOD is reduced, the flocs settle in a tank as activated sludge, a part of which is used as inoculum. (c) Tanks in which the rest of the activated sludge is digested by anaerobic bacteria, producing biogas (methane, H₂S, CO₂).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Name the two primate ancestors of present-day humans who existed about 15 million years ago. (b) According to geological records, when and where did Australopithecines live? (c) Give two differences between Homo habilis and Homo erectus.
questions.solution: (a) Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus. (b) About 2 million years ago, in the East African grasslands. (c) Homo habilis had a brain capacity of about 650–800 cc and probably did not eat meat. Homo erectus (about 1.5 million years ago) had a larger brain, about 900 cc, and probably ate meat.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Expand the following abbreviations used for modes of assisted reproductive technologies : ZIFT, ICSI, IUT, GIFT. (ii) Which one of them cannot be considered a procedure of IVF? Give reasons.
questions.solution: (i) ZIFT: zygote intra-fallopian transfer. ICSI: intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection. IUT: intra-uterine transfer. GIFT: gamete intra-fallopian transfer. (ii) GIFT: an ovum is transferred into the fallopian tube of a female who cannot produce one, and fertilisation occurs inside her body (in vivo), not in the laboratory.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Differentiate between : (i) perisperm and pericarp (ii) syncarpous and apocarpous pistil (iii) plumule and radicle
questions.solution: (i) Perisperm is residual, persistent nucellus in some seeds (e.g. black pepper, beet); pericarp is the fruit wall, developed from the ovary wall. (ii) A syncarpous pistil has fused carpels (e.g. Papaver, Hibiscus); an apocarpous pistil has free carpels (e.g. Michelia, lotus). (iii) The plumule is the embryonic shoot tip that forms the shoot; the radicle is the embryonic root tip that forms the root.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
How a gene is expressed in a cell, when it needs to be expressed, and how gene expression is regulated in a prokaryote was studied by Jacques Monod, a biochemist, and François Jacob, a geneticist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of the lac operon, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.

Why is the lac operon said to be a transcriptionally regulated system?
questions.solution: Its expression is controlled at the level of initiation of transcription: the repressor binding to the operator decides whether RNA polymerase can transcribe the structural genes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
How a gene is expressed in a cell, when it needs to be expressed, and how gene expression is regulated in a prokaryote was studied by Jacques Monod, a biochemist, and François Jacob, a geneticist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of the lac operon, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.

It is said that the lac operon has to be operational at a very low level in the bacterial cell all the time. Justify.
questions.solution: A low level of permease is needed for lactose to enter the cell at all; only then can lactose (allolactose) act as the inducer and switch the operon on.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
How a gene is expressed in a cell, when it needs to be expressed, and how gene expression is regulated in a prokaryote was studied by Jacques Monod, a biochemist, and François Jacob, a geneticist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of the lac operon, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.

Why is the regulator gene of the lac operon called the 'i' gene? Also explain how the lac operon works in the absence of an inducer.
questions.solution: The term 'i' comes from 'inhibitor': it codes for the repressor protein. Without an inducer, the repressor binds to the operator and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes z, y and a.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
How a gene is expressed in a cell, when it needs to be expressed, and how gene expression is regulated in a prokaryote was studied by Jacques Monod, a biochemist, and François Jacob, a geneticist. For their work on lactose metabolism in E. coli and introducing the concept of the lac operon, they were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1965.

Why is the regulator gene of the lac operon called the 'i' gene? Also explain how the lac operon works in the presence of an inducer.
questions.solution: The term 'i' comes from 'inhibitor': it codes for the repressor. When lactose (inducer) is present, it binds the repressor and inactivates it, so it cannot bind the operator; RNA polymerase then transcribes z, y and a, producing β-galactosidase, permease and transacetylase.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A diagram of the Earth shows region A as the band around the equator, roughly between 23.5° N and 23.5° S (the tropics), and region B as a band at high southern latitudes towards the pole.

Write the observations made regarding species diversity when moving from region A to region B. Give two reasons also.
questions.solution: Species diversity decreases from the equator (A) towards the poles (B). Reasons: the tropics have had a long evolutionary time with little disturbance (unlike temperate regions affected by glaciations); tropical environments are less seasonal and more constant and predictable, promoting niche specialisation; and they receive more solar energy, so productivity is higher.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A diagram of the Earth shows region A as the band around the equator, roughly between 23.5° N and 23.5° S (the tropics), and region B as a band at high southern latitudes towards the pole.

Stating the reason, mention the approximate number of bird species recorded in India.
questions.solution: About 1200 bird species, because India lies largely within tropical latitudes, which are rich in diversity (compared with about 105 in Greenland at a high latitude).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A diagram of the Earth shows region A as the band around the equator, roughly between 23.5° N and 23.5° S (the tropics), and region B as a band at high southern latitudes towards the pole.

Name the region of the world that records the greatest biodiversity and mention why.
questions.solution: The Amazonian rain forest in South America, the richest biodiversity on Earth, because of its tropical climate, high productivity and long undisturbed evolutionary history.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Meselson and Stahl carried out an experiment to prove the nature of DNA replication. (i) Which two types of nitrogen were used and why? (ii) Why did they take samples of E. coli at definite time intervals? (iii) State the role of the caesium chloride density gradient in their experiment. (iv) Write the conclusions they arrived at.
questions.solution: (i) ¹⁵N (heavy isotope) and ¹⁴N (normal). Growing E. coli on ¹⁵NH₄Cl for many generations made all DNA heavy; transferring to ¹⁴N let them follow how new strands were made, as DNA of different densities can be separated. (ii) E. coli divides about every 20 minutes, so samples at definite intervals give DNA after each round of replication. (iii) Centrifugation in a CsCl density gradient separates DNA molecules by density: heavy (¹⁵N), hybrid and light (¹⁴N). (iv) After one generation all DNA was hybrid; after two, half hybrid and half light. This proved DNA replicates semi-conservatively.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) A true-breeding tall pea plant with round seeds is crossed with a recessive dwarf pea plant with wrinkled seeds. Work out the cross up to the F₂ generation, giving the phenotypic ratios of the F₁ and F₂ generations. (ii) State the Mendelian principle that can be derived only with the help of such a cross.
questions.solution: (i) TTRR × ttrr → F₁ all TtRr (tall, round). F₁ selfed: gametes TR, Tr, tR, tr in equal proportions; F₂ phenotypes 9 tall round : 3 tall wrinkled : 3 dwarf round : 1 dwarf wrinkled. (ii) The law of independent assortment: when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair is independent of the other.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A graph shows antibody concentration in a child's blood after vaccination: a small rise and fall in the first 100 days, and then, on reinfection with the same pathogen at about 130 days, a rapid and much higher rise. (i) Explain why giving a vaccine increases the antibody concentration. (ii) If the child is infected with the same pathogen about four months later, the antibody concentration rises very fast. Explain why. (iii) Identify P, Q, R, S and T: natural active immunity – antibodies produced: yes – memory cells: P – mode: Q; natural passive – no – R – across the placenta or by breast feeding; acquired active – S – yes – getting a vaccine; acquired passive – T – no – injection of antibodies.
questions.solution: (i) The vaccine contains antigens (inactivated or weakened pathogens or their proteins), which trigger a primary immune response: B cells produce antibodies and memory cells form. (ii) Memory B and T cells recognise the pathogen quickly and produce a secondary (anamnestic) response, which is faster and stronger. (iii) P: yes; Q: by natural infection with the pathogen; R: no; S: yes; T: no.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) What is the chemical name of 'smack'? Why is the consumption of smack considered an abuse? (ii) Name the source plant and one effect of the following drugs on the human body : (1) marijuana (2) cocaine (3) morphine
questions.solution: (i) Diacetylmorphine (heroin). It is a depressant that slows down body functions, is highly addictive and is taken for non-medical purposes in quantities that impair physical, physiological and psychological functions, which is drug abuse. (ii)(1) Cannabis sativa; affects the cardiovascular system. (2) Erythroxylum coca; interferes with dopamine transport, stimulates the CNS producing euphoria and energy, and in excess causes hallucinations. (3) Papaver somniferum (latex); a strong sedative and painkiller.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A diagram shows three modes of pollen transfer: 1 within the same flower, 2 between two flowers of the same plant, 3 from a flower of one plant to a flower of another plant. (i) Write the technical terms for methods 1, 2 and 3. (ii) How do (1) water lily and (2) Vallisneria achieve pollination? (iii) Explain one hereditary and one physiological device that helps flowering plants avoid inbreeding depression.
questions.solution: (i) 1: autogamy; 2: geitonogamy; 3: xenogamy. (ii)(1) Water lily flowers emerge above the water and are pollinated by insects or wind. (2) Vallisneria female flowers reach the surface on long stalks; male flowers or pollen released onto the water are carried passively by currents to them. (iii) Hereditary: self-incompatibility, a genetic mechanism that prevents pollen of the same flower from fertilising its ovules. Physiological: pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised, or the anther and stigma are placed at different positions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A diagram shows the 28-day menstrual cycle of a normal human female. (i) What are the technical terms for (1) days 1–7 (2) days 8–12 (3) days 16–28 (4) days 13–15? (ii) Explain the role of ovarian and pituitary hormones during (1) days 8–12 (2) days 13–15 (3) days 16–28.
questions.solution: (i)(1) Menstrual phase. (2) Follicular (proliferative) phase. (3) Luteal (secretory) phase. (4) Ovulatory phase. (ii)(1) Pituitary FSH and LH rise gradually and stimulate follicular development; growing follicles secrete oestrogen, which regenerates the endometrium. (2) LH and FSH peak mid-cycle (LH surge), causing rupture of the Graafian follicle and release of the ovum (ovulation). (3) The corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone, which maintains the endometrium for implantation; if fertilisation does not occur, it degenerates and menstruation follows.
